newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian dlr orbits $0.78, lacks escape velocity.
newsitem.headline: Australian dlr orbits $0.78, lacks escape velocity.

text.p: The Australian dollar crept higher at a quiet midsession but lacked the momentum to escape its recent well worn range.
The currency recouped a little lost ground on the crosses as U.S. hedge funds chased US$/yen higher and traders reported buying interest for AUD/yen out of Tokyo.

But it was restrained by US$0.7815 resistance and soon settled down at 78 to await the Federal Budget at 7.30 pm (0930 GMT). Markets are looking for the government to take another step on the road to fiscal rectitude which, if delivered, should underpin offshore confidence in Australian assets.
By 12.00 pm (0200 GMT) the local dollar was in a holding pattern at US$0.7803/087 after gliding up from an early US$0.7789/94 and US$0.7775/80 late here Monday.
The gains still left it in the middle of the US$0.7720/7860 range held since early April and analysts emphasised it would have to clear US$0.7835 to enliven an essentially flat technical picture.

Weeks of aimless wandering had also left a residue of support and resistance levels including US$0.7775, US$0.7735 and US$0.7720 among the former and on the topside US$0.7815, US$0.7835 and US$0.7860.
On the crosses the local currency edged up to 93.25/35 yen from and early 92.83/93 and Monday's late 92.41/51, but was still far below the 99.00 level held early last week.

Sentiment was steadied somewhat by a rally, albeit modest, in US$/yen as the market reacted to more calming words from Japanese opfficials. In particular, a top Bank of Japan official said the bank needed more time to assess the economic outlook, a statement analysts took as an attempt to hose down speculation of an imminent hike in interest rates.
That helped the U.S. dollar bounce back to 119.55/60 after being as low as 118.75 at one stage this morning.
The local dollar alos regained ground on a broadly softer mark to stand at 1.3307/19 from 1.3121/35 late here Monday and rallied to 59.8 in trade weighted terms from 59.5.
On the domestic front, the Federal Budget has not had much fanfare in the markets but still promises to cement the fiscal improvement set in place by the tight budget of 1996/97.

Median expectations are the government will cut between A$1.5-2.0 billion from the underlying deficit for 1997/98 leaving a shortfall of around A$2.0 billion. The headline balance will be in surplus by around A$10 billion, thanks to privatisation receipts so there should be no net bond issuance.

Analysts expect the government to forecast a balanced underlying budget for 1998/99 or maybe even a small surplus. That would be a relatively impressive performance compared to the rest of the OECD and could take Australia a step closer to earning a credit upgrade for its foreign debt.

There were some concerns the Treasurer might rely too much on ambitious economic assumptions rather than proper spending and taxation measures and any certainly a GDP growth forecast of more than 4.0 percent would draw accusations of fudging.
Underlying inflation was likely to be estimated at around 2.5 percent, much in line with the RBA's thinking.
For the dollar a tight budget is not always positive in that it may provide scope for an easing in monetary policy.
However, in this case the Reserve Bank only last week said it saw no economic benefit in another rate cut and implied it had already taken the likely budget outcome into account in its decision.
If the budget does not disappoint in its fiscal credentials, therefore, dealers expected it be supportice of bonds and the dollar in the longer term.
